Chapter 18: The Government and the Macroeconomy

Learning goals

Governments spend between a third and more than half of GDP in the rich countries, and most of them have borrowed a lot. This chapter looks at the data on spending, taxes, deficits and debt, and at the accounting rules that tie them together. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • read the U.S. federal budget: where the money goes, where it comes from, and how large the deficit is, in percent of GDP and in dollars per person (Table 18.1);
  • use the flow budget constraint and the intertemporal budget constraint to compute next year’s debt, the primary and total deficits, and the taxes a given path of spending requires;
  • explain why the debt-GDP ratio falls when GDP grows faster than the interest rate, and split the changes in the U.S. ratio into deficits and growth;
  • compare government spending and debt across countries, and describe the fiscal problem of the twenty-first century: the rise of health spending;
  • in Python: write small accounting functions, reshape tables with melt and merge, draw a chart with two vertical axes, animate a bar chart, and compare two vintages of the same data.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

Model overview

Governments buy goods and services, pay transfers such as pensions, and pay interest on their debt. They finance all this with taxes and, when taxes fall short, by borrowing. This chapter has no new model to solve: it describes government budgets with data. Behind the data, though, there are a few accounting equations that hold in every year and every country. They link each year’s deficit to the change in the debt, and they tell us that what matters for a country’s ability to borrow is its debt relative to GDP, which depends on the interest rate and on how fast the economy grows.

Below we turn each of these equations into a small Python function, together with a few tools for the charts. The sections that follow use them to look at U.S. spending, revenue and debt, compare them with other countries, ask whether deficits crowd out private investment, and study the long-run projections that make health spending the fiscal problem of this century.

The flow budget constraint (equations 18.1 and 18.2)

In every period the government’s uses of funds must equal its sources of funds:

\[\underbrace{G_t + Tr_t + iB_t}_{\text{uses}} = \underbrace{T_t + \Delta B_{t+1} + \Delta M_{t+1}}_{\text{sources}}. \tag{18.1}\]

The government buys goods and services \(G_t\), pays transfers \(Tr_t\) (Social Security, unemployment insurance, welfare) and pays interest \(i\) on its debt \(B_t\). It gets the money from taxes \(T_t\), from new borrowing \(\Delta B_{t+1} = B_{t+1} - B_t\) and from printing money \(\Delta M_{t+1}\). As in the textbook, we set \(\Delta M_{t+1} = 0\) and count transfers inside \(G_t\). Then the constraint says how the debt moves:

\[B_{t+1} = (1+i)B_t + \underbrace{G_t - T_t}_{\text{primary deficit}}. \tag{18.2}\]

The primary deficit \(G_t - T_t\) leaves out the interest payments. The total deficit \(G_t + iB_t - T_t\) includes them, and it is the deficit that newspapers (and Table 18.1) report.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a one-line description. We write the interest rate as a decimal number, so 5 percent is 0.05.

def next_debt(B, G, T, i):
    """Equation (18.2): next period's debt, (1 + i) B + G - T."""
    return (1 + i) * B + G - T


def primary_deficit(G, T):
    """Primary deficit: spending minus taxes, leaving out the interest payments."""
    return G - T


def total_deficit(G, T, i, B):
    """Total deficit: spending plus the interest on the debt, minus taxes."""
    return G + i * B - T

A quick check: Exercise 5 of the textbook. A government owes 5 trillion dollars at an interest rate of 5 percent, and GDP (20 trillion dollars) grows by 4 percent a year. In case (a) it balances its primary budget (\(G = T\)). In case (b) it balances its total budget, so taxes also pay the interest.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each value in the list [1, 2, 3]. In each pass, B_a = next_debt(B_a, ...) replaces the old debt by the new one. An f-string such as f"{B_a:.3f}" puts a number into the text, here with 3 decimals.

i, g = 0.05, 0.04                      # interest rate and GDP growth rate
B_a, B_b, Y = 5.0, 5.0, 20.0           # debt in cases (a) and (b), and GDP, trillions of dollars
for year in [1, 2, 3]:
    T_b = 4.0 + i * B_b                # case (b): taxes cover spending of 4.0 and the interest
    print(f"Year {year}: (a) primary deficit {primary_deficit(4.0, 4.0):.2f}, total {total_deficit(4.0, 4.0, i, B_a):.3f}"
          f"   (b) primary deficit {primary_deficit(4.0, T_b):.2f}, total {total_deficit(4.0, T_b, i, B_b):.2f}")
    B_a = next_debt(B_a, G=4.0, T=4.0, i=i)
    B_b = next_debt(B_b, G=4.0, T=T_b, i=i)
    Y = (1 + g) * Y
    print(f"   debt (a) {B_a:.3f} = {100 * B_a / Y:.2f}% of GDP,  debt (b) {B_b:.3f} = {100 * B_b / Y:.2f}% of GDP")
Year 1: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.250   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.250 = 25.24% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 24.04% of GDP
Year 2: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.263   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.512 = 25.48% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 23.11% of GDP
Year 3: (a) primary deficit 0.00, total 0.276   (b) primary deficit -0.25, total 0.00
   debt (a) 5.788 = 25.73% of GDP,  debt (b) 5.000 = 22.22% of GDP

In case (a) the total deficit is the interest bill, so the debt grows at the interest rate, 5 percent a year. In case (b) the primary surplus of 0.25 trillion pays the interest, and the debt stays at 5 trillion. With a balanced primary budget the debt-GDP ratio rises from 25 percent by about 1 percent a year: 5 percent minus 4 percent. With a balanced total budget the ratio falls by about 4 percent a year, as GDP grows.

The intertemporal budget constraint (equations 18.5 and 18.6)

In a world that lasts two periods, all debt must be repaid by the end: \(B_3 = 0\). Combining the flow constraints of the two periods gives the intertemporal budget constraint:

\[\underbrace{G_1 + \frac{G_2}{1+i}}_{\text{pdv of spending}} + \underbrace{(1+i)B_1}_{\text{initial debt}} = \underbrace{T_1 + \frac{T_2}{1+i}}_{\text{pdv of taxes}}. \tag{18.5}\]

A future amount is worth less today, so we divide it by \(1+i\): that is its present discounted value (pdv). Moving the taxes to the left gives equation (18.6): the pdv of the budget balances \(T - G\) must pay off the initial debt \((1+i)B_1\). The budget must balance, not period by period, but in present value.

Here is a two-period example with the textbook’s initial debt of 25 trillion dollars. The government spends 7 trillion in each period, collects 5 trillion of taxes in period 1, and must find the taxes of period 2.

def pdv(first, second, i):
    """Present discounted value of an amount in period 1 and one in period 2 (equation 18.5)."""
    return first + second / (1 + i)


B1, i = 25.0, 0.05                     # initial debt (trillions of dollars) and interest rate
G1, G2, T1 = 7.0, 7.0, 5.0
B2 = next_debt(B1, G1, T1, i)          # equation (18.3): the debt at the start of period 2
T2 = (1 + i) * B2 + G2                 # equation (18.4) with B3 = 0: period-2 taxes repay everything
print(f"B2 = {B2:.2f}, so the period-2 taxes must be T2 = {T2:.2f} trillion dollars")
print(f"Uses:    pdv of spending {pdv(G1, G2, i):.3f} + initial debt {(1 + i) * B1:.3f} = "
      f"{pdv(G1, G2, i) + (1 + i) * B1:.3f}")
print(f"Sources: pdv of taxes {pdv(T1, T2, i):.3f}")
print(f"Equation (18.6): pdv of the budget balances {pdv(T1 - G1, T2 - G2, i):.3f} = (1 + i) B1")
B2 = 28.25, so the period-2 taxes must be T2 = 36.66 trillion dollars
Uses:    pdv of spending 13.667 + initial debt 26.250 = 39.917
Sources: pdv of taxes 39.917
Equation (18.6): pdv of the budget balances 26.250 = (1 + i) B1

The deficit of 2 trillion in period 1 and the inherited debt must both be paid with a large surplus in period 2: taxes of 36.66 trillion against spending of 7. Borrowing today means higher taxes in the future.

The debt-GDP ratio

What matters for a country’s ability to pay is not the debt in dollars but the debt relative to GDP, the tax base. Let nominal GDP grow at the rate \(g\), and write \(b = B/Y\) for the debt-GDP ratio and \(d\) for the primary deficit as a share of GDP. Dividing equation (18.2) by GDP gives

\[b_{\text{next}} = \frac{1+i}{1+g}\, b + d \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_{\text{next}} - b \approx d + (i - g)\, b.\]

The ratio rises with the primary deficit \(d\). It also rises when the interest rate is above the growth rate, and it falls when GDP grows faster than the interest rate, even with a balanced primary budget.

Python note. path = [] starts an empty list, and path.append(b) adds one value at its end. For a pandas Series with years as row labels, deficit.loc[1951:1974] keeps the years 1951 to 1974 (both included), and .sum() adds them up.

def next_debt_ratio(b, i, g, d):
    """Equation (18.2) divided by GDP: next year's debt ratio, (1 + i) / (1 + g) b + d."""
    return (1 + i) / (1 + g) * b + d


def debt_ratio_path(b, i, g, deficits):
    """The debt ratio after each year of a list of primary deficits (all in percent of GDP)."""
    path = []
    for d in deficits:
        b = next_debt_ratio(b, i, g, d)
        path.append(b)
    return path


def debt_change_parts(debt, deficit, start, end):
    """Split the change in the debt ratio from start to end into primary deficits and the rest."""
    change = debt[end] - debt[start]
    from_deficits = deficit.loc[start + 1:end].sum()
    return change, from_deficits, change - from_deficits

The ratio tool repeats case (a) of Exercise 5 without computing the debt and GDP separately:

case_a = debt_ratio_path(25.0, 0.05, 0.04, [0, 0, 0])      # a balanced primary budget for three years
print("Debt ratio, case (a):", np.round(case_a, 2))
print(f"Growth of the ratio: {100 * (case_a[0] / 25.0 - 1):.2f}% a year = 1.05 / 1.04 - 1")
Debt ratio, case (a): [25.24 25.48 25.73]
Growth of the ratio: 0.96% a year = 1.05 / 1.04 - 1

The part of a change that is not explained by primary deficits, change - from_deficits, is the effect of interest minus growth, \((i-g)\,b\), summed over the years. We use it on the U.S. data in Fig. 2.

Saving and investment (equation 18.7)

Adding and subtracting taxes in the national income identity splits total saving into three parts:

\[\underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM - EX)}_{\text{foreign saving}} = I. \tag{18.7}\]

Investment is financed by households and firms, by the government and by foreigners. A budget deficit is negative government saving, so private or foreign saving must fill the gap, or investment falls. That fall is called crowding out.

def private_and_foreign_saving(investment, government_saving):
    """Equation (18.7) solved for the saving of households, firms and foreigners: I - (T - G)."""
    return investment - government_saving

Tools for the data

Four small tools help with the figures. period_mean averages a series over some years, and add_period_means draws those averages on a chart. per_person turns a share of GDP into dollars per person. actual_and_projection and one_legend_entry prepare the long-run projections of Figs. 6 and 7, where actual data (solid lines) are followed by projections (dashed lines).

Python note. zip(columns, colors) hands over one (column, color) pair at a time to the loop. fig.add_vrect shades a band between two x values, and fig.add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a straight line between two points.

def period_mean(series, start, end):
    """Average of a Series with years as row labels, from start to end (both included)."""
    return series.loc[start:end].mean()


def add_period_means(fig, data, columns, colors, start, end):
    """Shade the years start-end and draw each column's average over them (Figs. 1 and 5)."""
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start - 0.5, x1=end + 0.5, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    for column, color in zip(columns, colors):
        mean = period_mean(data[column], start, end)
        fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start - 0.5, x1=end + 0.5, y0=mean, y1=mean,
                      line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash="dot"))
    return fig


def per_person(percent_of_gdp, gdp_billions, population_millions):
    """Dollars per person of a budget line given in percent of GDP (Table 18.1)."""
    return percent_of_gdp / 100 * gdp_billions * 1e9 / (population_millions * 1e6)

Python note. melt turns a wide table (one column per series) into a long one (one row per year and series), which is the shape Plotly Express likes. .map({0: ..., 1: ...}) replaces each value by its label, .copy() makes an independent copy, and pd.concat([a, b]) stacks two tables. trace.name.rsplit(", ", 1) cuts a text such as "Revenues, actual" at its last comma, into its two parts.

def actual_and_projection(data, names):
    """Long table for Figs. 6 and 7: one row per year and series, actual data and CBO projection.

    FY2025 is repeated in the projection, so that the dashed line starts where the solid line ends."""
    long = data.rename(columns=names).melt(id_vars=["year", "projection"], value_vars=list(names.values()),
                                           var_name="series", value_name="percent")
    long["segment"] = long.projection.map({0: "actual", 1: "CBO projection"})
    joint = long[long.year == 2025].copy()
    joint["segment"] = "CBO projection"
    return pd.concat([long, joint]).sort_values(["series", "segment", "year"])


def one_legend_entry(fig):
    """Plotly Express names each trace 'series, segment': keep one legend entry per series."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        series, segment = trace.name.rsplit(", ", 1)
        trace.update(name=series, legendgroup=series, showlegend=(segment == "actual"))
    return fig

U.S. spending, revenue and debt

We start with the U.S. federal budget: how much the government spends and collects, and how its deficits added up to the debt over the last century.

Fig. 1: U.S. federal government revenue and spending

Goal. See how large the federal government is, relative to the economy, and how its spending and revenue have changed since the 1930s.

The data are the federal outlays (spending) and receipts (revenue) as a percentage of GDP, from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). They are measured in fiscal years: the U.S. federal fiscal year 2025, for example, ran from October 2024 to September 2025.

revenue_spending = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-1.csv")
revenue_spending.tail(3)
year spending_gdp_pct revenue_gdp_pct
89 2023 22.4 16.2
90 2024 23.3 17.0
91 2025 23.1 17.3

spending_gdp_pct and revenue_gdp_pct are percentages of GDP, from FY1934 to FY2025. The menu draws the averages over one period as dotted lines. The textbook’s dashed lines at 18 and 20 percent stay on the chart.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend, and set_index("year") makes the years the row labels, as period_mean needs. PERIODS is a dictionary: each name (the key) gives a pair of years (the value), and start, end = PERIODS[period] unpacks the pair. fig.add_hline draws a horizontal line across the chart.

named = revenue_spending.rename(columns={"spending_gdp_pct": "Spending", "revenue_gdp_pct": "Revenue"})
by_year = named.set_index("year")
PERIODS = {"FY1934–1939": (1934, 1939), "FY1950–1969": (1950, 1969), "FY1970–1997": (1970, 1997),
           "FY1998–2001": (1998, 2001), "FY2002–2025": (2002, 2025), "FY1975–2024": (1975, 2024)}


def budget_chart(period="FY1950–1969"):
    """Fig. 18.1: federal spending and revenue (% of GDP), with their averages over one period."""
    start, end = PERIODS[period]
    spending, revenue = period_mean(by_year.Spending, start, end), period_mean(by_year.Revenue, start, end)
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Spending", "Revenue"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Fiscal year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{period}: spending averaged {spending:.1f}% and revenue {revenue:.1f}% of GDP")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    for level in [18, 20]:                       # the textbook's dashed reference lines
        fig.add_hline(y=level, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    add_period_means(fig, by_year, ["Spending", "Revenue"], [BLUE, GREEN], start, end)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1930, 2028])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 46], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Python note. interact calls budget_chart again whenever you choose another period in the Dropdown menu, and shows the figure it returns. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(budget_chart, period=Dropdown(options=list(PERIODS), value="FY1950–1969", description="period",
                                       style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(budget_chart, "period", ["FY1934–1939", "FY1950–1969", "FY1970–1997", "FY1998–2001",
                                       "FY2002–2025", "FY1975–2024"], start="FY1950–1969", label="period")

Source. Data: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables of the FY2027 Budget, Table 1.2, total receipts and total outlays as percentages of GDP. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • In the 1930s the federal government was small: revenue averaged 5.9 percent of GDP. World War II changed that. Spending peaked at 42.7 percent of GDP in FY1944, almost all of it for national defense.
  • In the two decades after the war, spending and revenue were both close to 17–18 percent of GDP, and the budget was roughly balanced (choose FY1950–1969).
  • From 1970 spending stayed above revenue in almost every year. FY1998–2001 were the exceptions, the only surpluses since 1969. Spending jumped in the Great Recession (FY2009) and in the Covid-19 pandemic (FY2020).
  • The textbook’s figure note says both averaged “about 20 percent” in recent decades. Choose FY1975–2024: spending averaged 21.1 percent, but revenue only 17.3 percent. That gap is the deficit of Fig. 2.

Key numbers: the war, the 1930s and the 20 percent ceiling

print(f"Highest spending: {by_year.Spending.max():.1f}% of GDP in FY{by_year.Spending.idxmax()}")
print(f"Revenue in FY1944: {by_year.Revenue[1944]:.1f}% of GDP")
print(f"Average revenue, FY1934-1939: {period_mean(by_year.Revenue, 1934, 1939):.1f}% of GDP")
print("Fiscal years with revenue of 20% of GDP or more:", by_year.index[by_year.Revenue >= 20].tolist())
print(f"FY2025: spending {by_year.Spending[2025]:.1f}%, revenue {by_year.Revenue[2025]:.1f}% of GDP")
Highest spending: 42.7% of GDP in FY1944
Revenue in FY1944: 20.5% of GDP
Average revenue, FY1934-1939: 5.9% of GDP
Fiscal years with revenue of 20% of GDP or more: [1944, 2000]
FY2025: spending 23.1%, revenue 17.3% of GDP

The textbook says spending peaked “at just under 44 percent” and revenue reached “nearly 21 percent” in 1944. Today’s OMB tables give 42.7 and 20.5 percent: GDP of the 1940s has since been revised up, so the shares are a little smaller. Revenue reached 20 percent of GDP only twice, in FY1944 and FY2000. This is the textbook’s “taxes have remained at or below 20 percent of GDP during virtually the entire history of the United States”.

Beyond the United States: government budgets in 38 countries

The federal budget is not the whole government: U.S. states and cities spend and tax, too. To compare countries we need general government, all levels together, which the OECD measures in the same way for every country. The file gov_finance.csv has, for 42 countries and calendar years, general government revenue, spending and the budget balance (revenue minus spending), and the private_investment that we use in Fig. 5, all in percent of GDP.

finance = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_finance.csv")
finance[finance.country == "United States"].tail(3)
iso3 country year revenue spending balance private_investment region
1376 USA United States 2022 34.70 38.42 -3.72 18.78 Americas
1377 USA United States 2023 31.26 39.21 -7.95 18.27 Americas
1378 USA United States 2024 31.53 39.57 -8.04 18.17 Americas

The series start in 1970 for the United States, Korea and Sweden, but only in 1995 for most European countries. Brazil and Costa Rica have investment data only: their OECD government accounts are about 24 points of GDP above the IMF’s numbers for the same concept, so we leave them out. China and South Africa report only the balance. That leaves 38 countries with revenue and spending. The chart function draws one country at a time.

Python note. .dropna(subset=["revenue", "spending"]) drops the rows in which one of these two columns is missing, and sorted(... .unique()) lists every remaining country once, in alphabetical order.

FINANCE_COUNTRIES = sorted(finance.dropna(subset=["revenue"]).country.unique())


def budget_by_country(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 18.1 for any country: general government spending and revenue (% of GDP, OECD)."""
    rows = finance[finance.country == country].dropna(subset=["revenue", "spending"])
    rows = rows.rename(columns={"spending": "Spending", "revenue": "Revenue"})
    title = f"{country}: no OECD data on government revenue and spending"
    if len(rows) > 0:
        title = (f"{country}, {rows.year.min()}–{rows.year.max()}: spending averaged {rows.Spending.mean():.1f}%, "
                 f"revenue {rows.Revenue.mean():.1f}% of GDP")
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y=["Spending", "Revenue"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1958, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 70], tickvals=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.99, y=1.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The widget below is the Colab version. The website version needs one precomputed chart per country, joined by a menu; the helper cell right after the widget builds it.

interact(budget_by_country, country=Dropdown(options=FINANCE_COUNTRIES, value="United States", description="country",
                                             style=WIDE));
Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions with a country menu (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, options, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(option) for every option and join the results with a dropdown menu.

    The website cannot run Python, so a figure with a country menu gets this precomputed version."""
    figures = [make_figure(o) for o in options]
    first = options.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range,
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(options[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", active=first, buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")],
                      margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: general government budgets in 38 countries, with a country menu
dropdown_figure(budget_by_country, FINANCE_COUNTRIES, start="United States")

Data: OECD national accounts, general government total revenue (OTR), total expenditure (OTE) and net lending (B9) (Table 12, dataflow DSD_NASEC10@DF_TABLE12), divided by GDP (Table 1, DSD_NAMAIN10@DF_TABLE1_EXPENDITURE); via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared file: data/ch18/gov_finance.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Pick a country in the menu above the chart.

What to notice.

  • The U.S. general government, federal plus state and local, spent 39.6 percent of GDP in 2024 and collected 31.5 percent: 16 and 15 points more than the federal budget alone (23.3 and 17.0 percent in FY2024). Fig. 3 compares countries with this general-government measure.
  • Choose France or Italy: spending was above revenue in every year since 1995. Sweden’s budget was balanced on average (14 surpluses in 31 years), at a much higher level of spending, about 52 percent of GDP.
  • Choose Norway: revenue above spending in 30 of 31 years, because the government collects the oil revenue. Choose Ireland: spending jumps to 65.0 percent of GDP in 2010, when the government rescued its banks.

Table 18.1: the federal budget in 2023 and 2025

Table 18.1 splits the budget into its main parts. The wider file federal_budget.csv has the same lines for every fiscal year since 1940, in percent of GDP, together with GDP (billions of dollars) and the population (millions, from 1960).

budget = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
budget[budget.year >= 2023][["year", "release", "gdp_billions", "population_millions", "total_spending",

There are two rows for 2023. The textbook was written in early 2023, before fiscal year 2023 was over, so its table shows OMB’s estimate from March 2023 (the row “estimate (FY2024 Budget)”). The actual numbers came in lower: spending 22.4 instead of 24.2 percent of GDP, revenue 16.2 instead of 18.2 percent.

Python note. budget[(budget.year == year) & (budget.release == release)] keeps the rows where both conditions are true, and .iloc[0] takes the first of them. round(-2) rounds to the nearest 100.

LINES = {"total_spending": "Total expenditures", "health": "Health (including Medicare)",
         "social_security": "Social Security", "defense": "National defense", "income_security": "Income security",
         "net_interest": "Net interest", "other_spending": "Other spending", "total_revenue": "Total revenues",
         "individual_income_tax": "Individual income taxes",
         "social_insurance_tax": "Social insurance and retirement receipts",
         "corporate_income_tax": "Corporate income taxes", "other_revenue": "Other revenues",
         "balance": "Budget balance (deficit < 0)"}


def budget_table(year, release="actual (FY2027 Budget)"):
    """Table 18.1 for one fiscal year: each line in percent of GDP and in dollars per person."""
    row = budget[(budget.year == year) & (budget.release == release)].iloc[0]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Percent of GDP": row[list(LINES)].astype(float)})
    table["Dollars per person"] = per_person(table["Percent of GDP"], row.gdp_billions,
                                             row.population_millions).round(-2)
    return table.rename(index=LINES)

We put the textbook’s numbers next to the estimate it used, the actual 2023 numbers and the latest year, 2025.

book = pd.DataFrame({"Textbook 2023, %": [23.9, 6.4, 5.1, 3.1, 3.0, 2.5, 3.9, 18.0, 8.7, 6.3, 2.0, 0.9, -5.9],

                                                1600, 800, -4700]},

Fig. 2: Federal debt and deficits in the United States

Goal. Follow the U.S. debt-GDP ratio and the budget surplus or deficit together, and see how the deficits of each year build up the debt.

The government debt is the stock of bonds the government has sold in the past and not yet repaid. Each year’s deficit adds to it. The data are the federal debt held by the public (outside the government), at the end of each fiscal year, and the total surplus (+) or deficit (−), both in percent of GDP.

debt_deficit = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-2.csv")
debt_deficit[debt_deficit.year.between(1937, 1942)]

.between(1937, 1942) is true for the years 1937 to 1942, so we see six rows. NaN (“not a number”) marks a missing value: OMB’s debt table starts in FY1940. The textbook’s figure has one more debt point, for 1939, from an older edition of the table. Plotly simply starts the debt line in 1940.

The two series differ a lot in size, so each gets its own vertical axis: the budget balance on the left and the debt on the right. We line up the zeros of the two axes, so that the dashed line marks zero on both.

Python note. fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(..., yaxis="y2")) adds a line that uses a second vertical axis. In update_layout, yaxis2=dict(overlaying="y", side="right", ...) puts that axis on the right, over the same plot. fig.add_annotation writes a label at a point of the chart; <br> starts a new line.

                         line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))

                   font=dict(color=BLUE, size=14))

                   font=dict(color=GREEN, size=14))

Sources. Data: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables of the FY2027 Budget, Table 1.2 (surplus or deficit as a percentage of GDP) and Table 7.1 (federal debt held by the public as a percentage of GDP). Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-2.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • To pay for World War II the government ran deficits of up to 29.6 percent of GDP (FY1943), and the debt rose to 106.1 percent of GDP in FY1946: more than one year of the economy’s whole output.
  • Over the next 30 years the ratio fell to 23.2 percent (FY1974). The budget was close to balance in most of those years, so the deficits do not explain this decline. Economic growth does, as the key numbers below show.
  • The deficits from the late 1970s raised the ratio to 47.9 percent by FY1993. The surpluses of FY1998–2001 lowered it to 31.5 percent. Then the Great Recession (a deficit of 9.8 percent of GDP in FY2009) and the pandemic (14.5 percent in FY2020) raised it to 98.5 percent, and it reached 99.5 percent in FY2025.

Key numbers: primary deficits and growth

How did the United States pay off its war debt? Fig. 6’s file has federal revenue and spending excluding interest from FY1950, so their difference is the primary balance. The total balance of Fig. 2 minus the primary balance is the interest paid. We first combine the two files.

Python note. merge(..., on="year") joins two tables row by row, matching the years. Rows whose year is missing in one of the tables are dropped, so the result starts in FY1950.

projections = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-6.csv")
history = debt_deficit.merge(projections[projections.projection == 0], on="year")
history["primary_deficit"] = history.spending_ex_interest - history.revenue
history["net_interest"] = -history.surplus_gdp_pct - history.primary_deficit
years = history.set_index("year")
years.loc[[1985, 1999, 2006, 2010, 2025], ["surplus_gdp_pct", "primary_deficit", "net_interest"]].round(2)
surplus_gdp_pct primary_deficit net_interest
year
1985 -5.0 1.95 3.05
1999 1.3 -3.77 2.47
2006 -1.8 0.21 1.59
2010 -8.7 7.41 1.29
2025 -5.9 2.62 3.28

These are the years of the textbook’s Exercise 3. In FY1999 the total surplus was 1.3 percent of GDP, but the primary surplus was much larger, 3.8 percent, because 2.5 percent of GDP went to interest. In FY2025 the total deficit was 5.9 percent, of which 3.3 percent was interest and only 2.6 percent primary deficit. (Table 18.1 shows 3.2 percent of interest: Fig. 2’s file rounds the deficit to one decimal, and the remainder takes the rounding.)

Now debt_change_parts splits the change in the debt ratio over four episodes.

EPISODES = [(1950, 1974), (1981, 1993), (2001, 2008), (2007, 2025)]
for start, end in EPISODES:
    change, from_deficits, rest = debt_change_parts(years.debt_public_gdp_pct, years.primary_deficit, start, end)
    print(f"FY{start}-{end}: debt ratio {change:+6.1f} points = primary deficits {from_deficits:+6.1f} "
          f"+ interest minus growth {rest:+6.1f}")
FY1950-1974: debt ratio  -55.4 points = primary deficits  -14.1 + interest minus growth  -41.3
FY1981-1993: debt ratio  +22.7 points = primary deficits  +14.6 + interest minus growth   +8.1
FY2001-2008: debt ratio   +7.7 points = primary deficits   +6.0 + interest minus growth   +1.7
FY2007-2025: debt ratio  +64.3 points = primary deficits  +80.5 + interest minus growth  -16.2

From FY1950 to FY1974 the debt ratio fell by 55.4 points. Primary surpluses paid for only 14.1 points of that. The other 41.3 points came from the term \((i-g)\,b\): nominal GDP grew faster than the interest rate on the debt, so the debt shrank relative to the economy. Growth, not repayment, paid off most of the war debt. In FY2007–2025, too, low interest rates and the inflation of 2021–23 offset 16.2 of the 80.5 points added by primary deficits.

Beyond the United States: two centuries of government debt

The IMF’s Public Finances in Modern History database collects the gross debt of the government, in percent of GDP, for 48 of our countries, in some cases back to 1800. Gross debt counts all government bonds and loans, also those held by other parts of the government, and it covers all levels of government where the data allow. So the U.S. line here lies above the federal debt held by the public of Fig. 2: by 15.1 points in 1946 and 24.9 points in 2024.

gross = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gross_debt.csv")
gross.head(3)
iso3 country year gross_debt region
0 ARG Argentina 1864 6.24 Americas
1 ARG Argentina 1865 6.62 Americas
2 ARG Argentina 1866 9.77 Americas

With many countries on one chart, each country needs its own color, and it should keep that color when we add or remove other countries. Two small tools do this for the multi-country charts of this notebook (Figs. 2, 4 and 8).

Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 is a list of 24 colors, and + joins two lists. enumerate numbers the items of a list as the loop runs (0, 1, 2, …), and i % len(PALETTE) is the remainder of the division, which starts again at 0 when the colors run out. colors.update(fixed) overwrites some entries of the dictionary. In latest_text, .groupby("country").tail(1) keeps the last row of each country, .iloc[[0, -1]] keeps the first and the last row of a table, and for i, (_, row) in enumerate(...) numbers the rows that .iterrows() hands over one at a time.

PALETTE = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Light24     # 48 distinct colors


def country_colors(names, fixed):
    """One fixed color per country, so that a country keeps its color when the selection changes."""
    colors = {}
    for i, name in enumerate(sorted(names)):
        colors[name] = PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)]
    colors.update(fixed)                        # the textbook's countries keep the colors of the book
    return colors


def latest_text(data, column, time):
    """The latest value of each chosen country, highest first; only the maximum and minimum for 3 or more."""
    if len(data) == 0:
        return "choose at least one country"
    last = data.sort_values(time).groupby("country").tail(1).sort_values(column, ascending=False)
    words = ["", ""]
    if len(last) > 2:
        last, words = last.iloc[[0, -1]], ["max ", "min "]
    parts = []
    for i, (_, row) in enumerate(last.iterrows()):
        parts.append(f"{words[i]}{row.country} {row[column]:.1f}")
    return "latest: " + ", ".join(parts)

The axes have two fixed sizes each: up to 150 percent of GDP, or up to 300 percent when a country above 150 percent is chosen; from 1900, or from 1800 when a chosen country’s data start earlier. list(range(50, top + 1, 50)) is the list of tick values 50, 100, … up to top.

GROSS_COLORS = country_colors(gross.country.unique(), {"United States": BLUE})


def gross_debt_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 18.2 for any countries: general government gross debt, percent of GDP (IMF)."""
    chosen = gross[gross.country.isin(countries)]
    top, start = 150, 1900
    if chosen.gross_debt.max() > 150:
        top = 300                               # a second, fixed scale for the most indebted countries
    if chosen.year.min() < 1900:
        start = 1800                            # some series start in the 19th century
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gross_debt", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=GROSS_COLORS, range_x=[start, 2027], range_y=[0, top],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gross_debt": "Percentage of GDP", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Gross debt, % of GDP, " + latest_text(chosen, "gross_debt", "year"))
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=list(range(50, top + 1, 50)))      # no 0 next to the first year
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The widget below is the Colab version. The website version draws all 48 countries at once, shows the United States, and keeps the others one click away; the helper cell right after the widget does this for every multi-country chart.

Python note. SelectMultiple is a list in which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click. The function then receives a tuple of names, such as ("United States", "Japan").

interact(gross_debt_chart,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(gross.country.unique()), value=("United States",), rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));
Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the multi-country website figures (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]


def legend_menu(fig, data, shown):
    """Website version of a multi-country chart: the countries in `shown` are drawn, every other country is
    one click away in the legend, and buttons show a group (the textbook's countries, the G7, a region, all).
    Traces that are not countries, such as averages, always stay visible."""
    countries = set(data.country)
    groups = {"Textbook": list(shown), "G7": G7}
    for region in sorted(data.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(data[data.region == region].country.unique())
    groups["All"] = list(countries)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.name in countries and trace.name not in shown:
            trace.visible = "legendonly"
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            visible.append(True if trace.name not in countries or trace.name in members else "legendonly")
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", pad=dict(r=4, t=0))],
                      margin=dict(t=120))
    return fig

fig.update_layout(title="Gross government debt in 48 countries, percent of GDP (IMF)", height=560)
legend_menu(fig, gross, ["United States"])

Click a country in the legend to add or remove it, or a button to show a group of countries.

What to notice.

  • Add the United Kingdom: its debt reached 260 percent of GDP after the Napoleonic wars (1821) and 270 percent after World War II (1946). By 2007 it was down to 43 percent, mostly through growth, as in the United States.
  • Japan’s debt rose to 258 percent of GDP in 2020 (237 percent in 2024), the highest of any rich country. Italy (135 percent) and Greece (155 percent) are also above the U.S. level of 122 percent in 2024.
  • Look at your data: the series start in different years (1929 for the U.S., 1984 for China), and some have holes. Germany has no values for 1914–1924 and 1939–1949, the years of the two world wars and the hyperinflation, and Plotly simply joins the points on either side of a hole with a straight line.

Spending and debt around the world

Is the U.S. government big or small? These figures compare government spending and debt across rich countries.

Fig. 3: Government spending around the world, 2019

Goal. Compare the size of government, at all levels (federal, state and local), across rich countries.

The OECD measures general government spending, which adds up the spending of the central, state and local governments. The textbook uses 2019, the last year before the pandemic. The data file adds the latest year available for all six countries, 2024.

spending = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-3.csv")
spending

Python note. melt stacks the two year columns into one column of values, with a new column that says which year each value belongs to. barmode="group" puts the bars of the two years side by side, and texttemplate="%{y:.1f}" writes each bar’s value above it.

bars = spending.melt(id_vars=["iso3", "country"], value_vars=["gov_spending_2019", "gov_spending_2024"],
                     var_name="year", value_name="gov_spending")
bars["year"] = bars.year.map({"gov_spending_2019": "2019 (textbook year)", "gov_spending_2024": "2024 (latest)"})
fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="gov_spending", color="year", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
             color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, LIGHT_BLUE], range_y=[0, 62],
             labels={"country": "Country", "gov_spending": "Percentage of GDP", "year": "Year"},
             title="General government spending: from 32% of GDP in Korea to 55% in France (2019)")
fig.update_traces(texttemplate="%{y:.1f}", textposition="outside")
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
fig.show()

Source. Data: OECD, Government at a Glance, general government expenditure as a percentage of GDP (dataflow DSD_GOV@DF_GOV_PF_YU, measure GE), via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-3.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • In 2019 the governments of France and Sweden spent about half of GDP or more, those of the U.S., Japan and South Korea well under 40 percent. The U.S., at 38.2 percent, is among the lowest of the rich countries.
  • In 2024 spending was higher than in 2019 in all six countries, by 0.6 points in Sweden up to 5.7 points in the U.K. (46.2 percent).

Data revisions: the same year, different numbers

The textbook’s bars for 2019 are not the same as ours. Statistical offices revise their data for years, for example when they measure GDP better. We compare the textbook’s values with today’s.

textbook = pd.Series({"S. Korea": 33.9, "Japan": 38.9, "U.S.": 38.4, "U.K.": 40.8, "Sweden": 49.1, "France": 55.3})
compare = spending.set_index("country")[["gov_spending_2019"]]
compare["textbook"] = textbook
compare["revision"] = compare.gov_spending_2019 - compare.textbook
compare.round(1)
gov_spending_2019 textbook revision
country
S. Korea 31.9 33.9 -2.0
Japan 37.8 38.9 -1.1
U.S. 38.2 38.4 -0.2
U.K. 40.5 40.8 -0.3
Sweden 49.8 49.1 0.7
France 55.3 55.3 0.0

Korea’s 2019 spending has been revised down by 2.0 points and Japan’s by 1.1 points. With today’s data, Japan spends a little less than the U.S., so the two bars have swapped places. The 2023 edition of the OECD data, which the textbook used, reproduces all six printed bars within 0.1 point.

All OECD countries, 2007–2024

The wider file gov_spending.csv has the same measure for all 38 OECD countries from 2007. The animation shows one year at a time. The countries stay in their 2019 order, so you can watch a bar grow or shrink.

Python note. oecd.iso3.isin(EURO_FOUR) is true for the rows whose code is in the list, and oecd.loc[rows, "group"] = ... changes the column group in those rows only. animation_frame="year" draws one chart per year and adds a play button and a slider. category_orders fixes the order of the countries on the x-axis. .sort_values(...) sorts a table, and .tolist() turns a column into a plain Python list.

Goal. Compare the government debt of five large rich countries since 1995.

This figure uses net debt: the debt of all levels of government minus the financial assets they own, in percent of GDP. For some countries, such as Norway with its large oil fund, net debt is negative.

Sources. Data: OECD government financial balance sheets, general government net financial worth (BF90, dataflow DSD_NASEC20@DF_T720GOV_A), divided by GDP (OECD Table 1, DSD_NAMAIN10@DF_TABLE1_EXPENDITURE); for Japan in 1995–2005, the OECD Economic Outlook net financial liabilities (GNFLQ); all via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-4.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Japan’s net debt rose from 18 percent of GDP in 1995 to a peak of 124 percent in 2020. Italy’s peaked at 152 percent in 2020, the U.S. ratio at 122 percent. Germany’s is the exception: after 2011 it fell, to 22 percent in 2025.
  • The textbook’s data end in 2021. Since then several ratios fell sharply, for example the U.K.’s from 101 to 68 percent in one year (2021 to 2022). These are stocks of assets and debts valued at market prices, so they move with interest rates and asset prices, not only with deficits. When interest rates jumped in 2022, the market value of old low-interest bonds fell, and high inflation raised nominal GDP. Both lowered the ratios, most likely more than any change in the deficits.

Data check: a number in the textbook that the data do not support

debt_table = net_debt.set_index("year")
print(f"Japan, Economic Outlook series: 1995 {debt_table.japan_eo[1995]:.1f}%, 2005 {debt_table.japan_eo[2005]:.1f}%")
print(f"Japan, balance sheets: 2021 {debt_table.japan[2021]:.1f}%, peak {debt_table.japan.max():.1f}% "
      f"in {debt_table.japan.idxmax()}, 2023 {debt_table.japan[2023]:.1f}%")
print(f"Italy 2021: {debt_table.italy[2021]:.1f}%   Germany 2021: {debt_table.germany[2021]:.1f}%")
Japan, Economic Outlook series: 1995 18.3%, 2005 66.2%
Japan, balance sheets: 2021 120.1%, peak 123.8% in 2020, 2023 93.7%
Italy 2021: 141.1%   Germany 2021: 33.7%

The textbook says in one place that Japan’s ratio rose to “more than 126 percent in 2021” and, in another, to “more than 140 percent in 2023”. Neither series reaches 140 percent: in 2023 Japan’s net debt was 93.7 percent of GDP. (The gross debt, before subtracting the government’s assets, is much higher, which may explain the second number.) When two numbers in a text disagree, check them in the data.

Beyond the five countries: net debt in 39 countries

The file net_debt.csv has the same OECD measure for 39 countries, one row per country and year, from 1995. Japan starts in 2005 here, as in the balance sheets above, and the 2025 values are not yet in for every country. The chart starts with the textbook’s five countries in the textbook’s colors. The vertical axis keeps the textbook’s scale unless a chosen country leaves it; then it switches to a wider fixed scale, and to a much wider one for Norway.

world_debt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "net_debt.csv")
BOOK_FIVE = ("Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States")
NET_COLORS = country_colors(world_debt.country.unique(), {"Italy": GREEN, "Japan": ORANGE, "United States": BLUE,
                                                         "United Kingdom": LIGHT_BLUE, "Germany": DARK_TEAL})


def net_debt_chart(countries=BOOK_FIVE):
    """Fig. 18.4 for any countries: net government debt, percent of GDP (OECD)."""
    chosen = world_debt[world_debt.country.isin(countries)]
    low, high = 0, 175
    if chosen.net_debt.min() < 0 or chosen.net_debt.max() > 175:
        low, high = -100, 200                   # a wider fixed scale for countries with negative net debt
    if chosen.net_debt.min() < -100:
        low = -450                              # Norway owns more than four years of GDP
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="net_debt", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=NET_COLORS, range_x=[1994, 2026.5], range_y=[low, high],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "net_debt": "Percentage of GDP", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Net debt, % of GDP, " + latest_text(chosen, "net_debt", "year"))
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(net_debt_chart,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world_debt.country.unique()), value=BOOK_FIVE, rows=8,

# Your turn: try it here

Deficits and private investment

When the government borrows, does it take saving away from private investment? Here we compare the U.S. budget balance with the private investment rate.

Fig. 5: U.S. private investment and the budget deficit

Goal. Ask whether budget deficits crowd out investment, using equation (18.7).

The data are gross private domestic investment and government saving (the federal budget balance, from the national accounts), both in percent of GDP, for calendar years.

saving = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-5.csv")
saving.head(3)
year investment_share gov_saving_share
0 1960 15.9441 0.028854
1 1961 15.4006 -0.841679
2 1962 16.0579 -0.889230

Equation (18.7) says that investment minus government saving is the saving of households, firms and foreigners. Our function private_and_foreign_saving computes it, and the chart hides it until you click its name in the legend. The buttons compare the averages before and after 1980.

named_saving = saving.rename(columns={"investment_share": "Investment", "gov_saving_share": "Government saving"})
named_saving["Private + foreign saving"] = private_and_foreign_saving(named_saving.Investment,
                                                                      named_saving["Government saving"])
saving_by_year = named_saving.set_index("year")
SPLITS = {"1960–1979": (1960, 1979), "1980–2025": (1980, 2025)}


def saving_chart(period="1980–2025"):
    """Fig. 18.5: investment and government saving (% of GDP), with their averages over one period."""
    start, end = SPLITS[period]
    I, S = period_mean(saving_by_year.Investment, start, end), period_mean(saving_by_year["Government saving"], start, end)
    fig = px.line(named_saving, x="year", y=["Investment", "Government saving", "Private + foreign saving"],
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, GRAY], range_y=[-15, 35],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{period}: investment averaged {I:.1f}%, government saving {S:.1f}% of GDP")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Private + foreign saving"), visible="legendonly", line_dash="dash")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    add_period_means(fig, saving_by_year, ["Investment", "Government saving"], [BLUE, GREEN], start, end)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026.5])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.57, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(saving_chart, period=ToggleButtons(options=list(SPLITS), value="1980–2025", description="averages over"));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(saving_chart, "period", ["1960–1979", "1980–2025"], start="1980–2025", label="averages over")

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, national accounts, via FRED: gross private domestic investment (GPDI), net federal government saving (FGDEF) and GDP (GDP). Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-5.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Government saving fell: from −2.2 percent of GDP on average in 1960–1979 to −4.1 percent in 1980–2025. Yet investment did not fall. It averaged 17.3 percent before 1980 and 17.7 percent after.
  • From year to year the two lines move together: from the early 1990s to 2000 government saving rose from −5.1
    1. to +1.6 percent of GDP, and investment from 15.3 (1991) to 19.9 percent. In 2009 both fell.
  • Click “Private + foreign saving” in the legend. By equation (18.7) it is the gap between the two lines. It rose when deficits grew, to 31.4 percent of GDP in 2020: households, firms and foreigners filled most of the gap left by the government, so the crowding out was small.

Key numbers: how strongly do the two lines move together?

The textbook speaks of “some correlation in the year-to-year movements”. A correlation of 1 means two series move exactly together, 0 means no relation.

Python note. .diff() takes the change from the previous year, and a.corr(b) is the correlation of two Series.

I, S = saving_by_year.Investment, saving_by_year["Government saving"]
print(f"Correlation of the levels:            {I.corr(S):.2f}")
print(f"Correlation of the changes each year: {I.diff().corr(S.diff()):.2f}")
for start, end in SPLITS.values():
    print(f"{start}-{end}: investment {period_mean(I, start, end):.2f}%, government saving "
          f"{period_mean(S, start, end):.2f}%, private + foreign saving "
          f"{period_mean(saving_by_year['Private + foreign saving'], start, end):.2f}%")
Correlation of the levels:            0.29
Correlation of the changes each year: 0.55
1960-1979: investment 17.25%, government saving -2.19%, private + foreign saving 19.44%
1980-2025: investment 17.72%, government saving -4.14%, private + foreign saving 21.86%

The changes are clearly correlated (0.55), the levels much less (0.29). In the short run, a larger deficit comes with lower investment. Over decades, private and foreign saving rose by 2.4 points of GDP and covered the larger deficits. The textbook’s estimate is that private saving offsets “no more than 50 cents” of each dollar of deficit; Chapter 19 looks at the foreign part.

Beyond the United States: investment and budget balances in 36 countries

Do the two lines move together in other countries, too? finance, from Fig. 1, has private investment and the general government budget balance (revenue minus spending, called net lending in the national accounts) for 36 countries. Private investment is all fixed investment except the government’s, plus inventories; for the United States it is within 0.4 points of GDP of the BEA series above. The budget balance is a little different from government saving: it also subtracts the government’s own investment. The title reports the correlation of the yearly changes, as in the key numbers above.

BALANCE_COUNTRIES = sorted(finance.dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"]).country.unique())


def crowding_out_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 18.5 for any country: private investment and the general government budget balance (% of GDP)."""
    rows = finance[finance.country == country].dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"])
    rows = rows.rename(columns={"private_investment": "Private investment", "balance": "Budget balance"})
    corr = rows["Private investment"].diff().corr(rows["Budget balance"].diff())
    low, high = -20, 35
    if rows["Budget balance"].min() < -18 or rows["Private investment"].max() > 33:
        low, high = -35, 55                     # a second, fixed scale for the extreme years
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y=["Private investment", "Budget balance"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  range_x=[1968, 2027], range_y=[low, high],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}, {rows.year.min()}–{rows.year.max()}: correlation of the yearly changes {corr:.2f}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.99, y=1.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(crowding_out_chart, country=Dropdown(options=BALANCE_COUNTRIES, value="United States", description="country",
                                              style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: investment and the budget balance in 36 countries, with a country menu
dropdown_figure(crowding_out_chart, BALANCE_COUNTRIES, start="United States")

Sources. Data: OECD national accounts, general government net lending (B9, Table 12, dataflow DSD_NASEC10@DF_TABLE12); OECD National Accounts at a Glance, Chapter 3, investment and the government’s share of it (DSD_NAAG@DF_NAAG_III); GDP and changes in inventories (Table 1, DSD_NAMAIN10@DF_TABLE1_EXPENDITURE); all via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared file: data/ch18/gov_finance.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Pick a country in the menu above the chart.

What to notice.

  • With the general government balance, the U.S. correlation of the yearly changes is 0.62, close to the 0.55 of the federal measure above.
  • The correlation is positive in all 36 countries (median 0.41), from 0.01 in Colombia to 0.75 in Japan. In a recession investment falls, and so do tax revenues, while spending rises: both lines drop together. A positive correlation therefore does not prove that deficits crowd out investment; the business cycle moves both.
  • Choose Ireland: the budget balance fell to −32.2 percent of GDP in 2010, when the government rescued its banks, and investment jumped to 51.5 percent of GDP in 2019 for the accounting reason explained in Chapter 17.

Your turn. Compute the averages for 2010–2019 and for 2020–2025. Did investment fall when the deficits of the pandemic years arrived? Then choose Germany in the menu: was its budget balance positive or negative on average from 2010 to 2019?

period_mean(I, 2010, 2019) and period_mean(I, 2020, 2025), and the same with S. For Germany, keep its rows with finance[finance.country == "Germany"], set the index to "year" and use period_mean on the balance column.

The fiscal problem of the twenty-first century

The last section looks ahead. Official projections show federal spending rising faster than revenue, driven mostly by health care, and health spending is rising in every rich country.

Fig. 6: U.S. federal spending and revenues, 1950–2075

Goal. See the fiscal problem of the twenty-first century: entitlement spending keeps rising, while revenue stays near 18 percent of GDP.

The textbook’s figure combines actual data up to 2000 with projections that the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) made in 2002, up to 2075. Our file has OMB’s actual numbers up to FY2025 and CBO’s newest long-term projections, from February 2026, which end in 2056. The column projection is 1 for the projected years. Figs. 6 and 7 stay U.S.-only: they show the CBO’s projections, which cover only the U.S. federal budget.

projections.tail(3)
year revenue spending_ex_interest ss_medicare_medicaid projection
104 2054 18.704 20.882 13.938 1
105 2055 18.741 20.943 14.008 1
106 2056 18.798 21.002 14.076 1

ss_medicare_medicaid is the spending on the three big entitlement programs: Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid (with CHIP and the health insurance tax credits, as CBO counts them). Like the textbook, we draw the spending excluding interest. We add the textbook’s CBO 2002 projections, read from its figure every ten years, as markers.

fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
for name, color in COLORS_6.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cbo_2002.year, y=cbo_2002[name], mode="markers", marker=dict(color=color, size=9,
                             symbol="x"), name="CBO 2002 (textbook)", legendgroup="2002",
                             showlegend=(name == "Revenues")))
fig.add_vrect(x0=2025, x1=2056, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
fig.update_xaxes(range=[1945, 2080])
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 31], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
fig.show()

Sources. Data: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables of the FY2027 Budget, Tables 1.2 (revenue and GDP), 3.1 (outlays and net interest) and 8.5 (mandatory programs); Congressional Budget Office, The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056, February 2026 for the projections. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-6.csv (see the data notes). The CBO 2002 markers are read from the textbook’s figure (CBO, A 125-Year Picture of the Federal Government’s Share of the Economy, 1950 to 2075, 2002). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Entitlement spending grew from 0.3 percent of GDP in 1950 to 7.1 percent in 2000 and 11.2 percent in 2025. It is now more than half of all non-interest spending, and CBO projects 14.1 percent by 2056.
  • Revenue has stayed between 14 and 20 percent of GDP for 75 years, and CBO projects 17.5 to 18.8 percent. Spending excluding interest stays above it, at about 20 to 21 percent: a primary deficit of about 2 percent of GDP in every projected year.
  • The new projection is much flatter than CBO’s 2002 projection (the markers): non-interest spending of 21.0 percent in 2056, against about 24.5 percent projected for the same year in 2002. Click “CBO 2002 (textbook)” to hide the markers. But actual spending since 2002 was far above the old projection, in 2009–12 and in 2020–21.

What the projection means for the debt

The projected primary deficits are not zero, so the debt keeps growing. How fast the ratio grows depends on the interest rate \(i\) and on the growth rate of nominal GDP \(g\), through debt_ratio_path. The sliders also let you cut the primary deficit in every year from FY2026, by raising taxes or cutting spending: the two “possible solutions” of the textbook.

Python note. max(path) and min(path) are the largest and smallest values of a list, and max(250, ...) is the larger of two numbers: the vertical axis stays at 0 to 250 unless the debt ratio would leave it. [50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None is a one-line if: it gives the list of ticks when the axis has its usual size, and None (let Plotly choose) when it has grown.

cbo = projections[projections.projection == 1]
cbo_deficits = (cbo.spending_ex_interest - cbo.revenue).tolist()     # projected primary deficits, FY2026-2056
b_2025 = debt_by_year[2025]
debt_history = debt_deficit[debt_deficit.year >= 1940]


def debt_projection(i=4.0, g=4.0, cut=0.0):
    """The debt ratio after FY2025 under CBO's primary deficits minus a cut (all in percent of GDP)."""
    deficits = []
    for d in cbo_deficits:
        deficits.append(d - cut)
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    top = max(250, 1.05 * max(path))                 # fixed axis, widened only when the debt ratio would leave it
    bottom = min(0, 1.1 * min(path))                 # below zero, the government owns more than it owes
    fig = px.line(debt_history, x="year", y="debt_public_gdp_pct", range_y=[bottom, top],
                  labels={"year": "Fiscal year", "debt_public_gdp_pct": "Debt held by the public (% of GDP)"},
                  title=f"Debt in FY2056: {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP (FY2025: {b_2025:.1f}%), "
                        f"average primary deficit {np.mean(deficits):.2f}%")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cbo.year, y=path, name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3, dash="dash"),
                             showlegend=False))
    fig.add_hline(y=b_2025, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=2025, x1=2056, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1938, 2058])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None)
    return fig
interact(debt_projection,
         i=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP growth g (%)", style=WIDE),
         cut=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="deficit cut (% of GDP)", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: the debt projection with a precomputed slider for the deficit cut (i = g = 4%)
slider_figure(debt_projection, "cut", [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0], start=0.0, label="deficit cut (% of GDP)")

Sources. Data: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 7.1 (debt held by the public); Congressional Budget Office, The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056 (primary deficits, revenue minus spending excluding interest). Prepared files: data/ch18/fig18-2.csv, data/ch18/fig18-6.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by the discussion of Fig. 18.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With \(i = g\) the interest and growth effects cancel, and the ratio simply adds up the primary deficits: from 99.5 percent of GDP in FY2025 to about 164 percent in FY2056.
  • Set the interest rate one point above growth (\(i = 5\), \(g = 4\)): the debt now grows faster than GDP even without deficits, and the ratio ends at 209 percent. One point below (\(i = 3\)), the same deficits give 130 percent. This is the “magic elixir” of growth from Fig. 2, working in either direction.
  • With \(i = g\), a cut of about 2 percent of GDP in every year, the size of the average primary deficit, keeps the ratio near its FY2025 level.

Key numbers: the projection in numbers

cbo_2056 = cbo.set_index("year").loc[2056]
print(f"FY2056 (CBO): revenue {cbo_2056.revenue:.1f}%, spending excluding interest {cbo_2056.spending_ex_interest:.1f}%, "
      f"entitlements {cbo_2056.ss_medicare_medicaid:.1f}% of GDP")
print(f"Average primary deficit FY2026-2056: {np.mean(cbo_deficits):.2f}% of GDP, sum {np.sum(cbo_deficits):.1f} points")
for i in [3.0, 4.0, 5.0]:
    print(f"i = {i}%, g = 4%: debt in FY2056 {debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, 0.04, cbo_deficits)[-1]:.1f}% of GDP")
FY2056 (CBO): revenue 18.8%, spending excluding interest 21.0%, entitlements 14.1% of GDP
Average primary deficit FY2026-2056: 2.09% of GDP, sum 64.7 points
i = 3.0%, g = 4%: debt in FY2056 129.9% of GDP
i = 4.0%, g = 4%: debt in FY2056 164.2% of GDP
i = 5.0%, g = 4%: debt in FY2056 208.8% of GDP

The textbook’s CBO 2002 projections had entitlements at 21.1 percent of GDP and total spending at nearly 40 percent by 2075. The 2026 projections are lower, but they tell the same story: under current policies spending stays above revenue, and the debt ratio keeps rising.

Sources. Data: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables of the FY2027 Budget, Tables 1.2 (revenue and GDP), 3.1 (outlays and net interest) and 8.5 (mandatory programs); Congressional Budget Office, The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056, February 2026 for the projections. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-7.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • All other spending fell from about 13–14 percent of GDP before 1980 to 8.4 percent in 2000. It jumped in the two crises (17.7 percent in 2020) and is projected to fall to 6.9 percent by 2056.
  • Social Security rose to about 4 percent of GDP by 1980, is 5.2 percent today, and is projected to level off near 6 percent.
  • Medicare and Medicaid started in the mid-1960s and keep rising: 3.1 percent of GDP in 2000, 6.0 percent in 2025 and 8.1 percent projected for 2056. In the textbook’s 2002 projection health reached 14.9 percent by 2075, but the direction is the same: health is the part of the budget that grows.

Key numbers: Social Security and health

The case study in the textbook says that Social Security spending will rise “from about 4.2 percent of GDP to about 6 percent”. Some combination of higher taxes and lower benefits must cover that gap.

by_part = components.set_index("year")
print(f"Social Security: 2000 {by_part.social_security[2000]:.2f}%, 2025 {by_part.social_security[2025]:.2f}%, "
      f"2030 {by_part.social_security[2030]:.2f}%, 2056 {by_part.social_security[2056]:.2f}%")
print(f"Medicare and Medicaid: 2000 {by_part.medicare_medicaid[2000]:.2f}%, 2030 {by_part.medicare_medicaid[2030]:.2f}%, "
      f"2056 {by_part.medicare_medicaid[2056]:.2f}%")
crossing = by_part.index[by_part.medicare_medicaid > by_part.other_ex_interest]
print(f"First year in which health spending exceeds all other spending: {crossing[0]}")
Social Security: 2000 4.01%, 2025 5.19%, 2030 5.57%, 2056 5.99%
Medicare and Medicaid: 2000 3.10%, 2030 6.04%, 2056 8.09%
First year in which health spending exceeds all other spending: 2041

Social Security goes from 4.0 percent of GDP in 2000 to 5.6 percent in 2030 and 6.0 percent in 2056, close to the textbook’s 4.2 → 6.2 → level. Medicare and Medicaid go from 3.1 percent to 6.0 percent in 2030 and 8.1 percent in 2056: slower than the 2002 projection (7.7 percent in 2030), but still rising when Social Security has stopped.

Fig. 8: Health spending as a share of GDP in five countries

Goal. Show that the rise of health spending is not only a U.S. problem.

The data are the total current health expenditure, public and private, as a percentage of GDP, from the OECD Health Statistics.

health = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-8.csv")
health.isna().sum()
year        0
usa         0
germany     1
france     16
japan       0
uk          0
dtype: int64

Some values are missing: France reports only every five years before 1990, and Germany has no value for 1991, the year after reunification. If we plotted the wide table, France’s line would have holes. After melt, we drop the missing rows with .dropna(), so that each line connects the years that do exist. The OECD’s current data start in 1970, so the textbook’s points for 1960 and 1965 cannot be drawn, and the 2025 values are provisional estimates.

NAMES_8 = {"usa": "U.S.", "germany": "Germany", "france": "France", "japan": "Japan", "uk": "U.K."}
health_long = health.rename(columns=NAMES_8).melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country",
                                                  value_name="health_share").dropna()
other_four = health.dropna()[["germany", "france", "japan", "uk"]].mean(axis=1)   # only years with all four
fig = px.line(health_long, x="year", y="health_share", color="country", hover_name="country", range_y=[2, 20],
              color_discrete_map={"U.S.": BLUE, "Germany": DARK_TEAL, "France": GREEN, "Japan": ORANGE,
                                  "U.K.": LIGHT_BLUE},
              labels={"year": "Year", "health_share": "Percent of GDP", "country": "Country"},
              title=f"U.S. health spending: {health.usa.iloc[0]:.1f}% of GDP in 1970, {health.usa.iloc[-1]:.1f}% in 2025")
fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=health.dropna().year, y=other_four, name="Average of the other four",
                         line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dot")))
fig.update_xaxes(range=[1968, 2027])
fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20])
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
fig.show()

Source. Data: OECD Health Statistics, System of Health Accounts, current health expenditure as a percentage of GDP (dataflow DSD_SHA@DF_SHA), via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared file: data/ch18/fig18-8.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Health spending rose in all five countries, as a share of GDP. In the U.S. it nearly tripled, from 6.2 percent in 1970 to 17.6 percent in 2025. The average of the other four rose from 4.8 to about 11–12 percent.
  • The U.S. pulled away from the others in the 1980s. Since 2010 its share has stayed near 16–18 percent. Japan and the U.K., the lowest spenders until 2010, came close to Germany and France.
  • The pandemic shows as a spike in 2020 (U.S. 18.7 percent, U.K. 12.0 percent): health spending rose and GDP fell at the same time.

Key numbers: why health spending rises

first_year, last_year = health.set_index("year").loc[1970], health.set_index("year").loc[2025]
growth = 100 * ((last_year / first_year) ** (1 / 55) - 1)        # average growth of the share, percent a year
pd.DataFrame({"1970": first_year, "2021": health.set_index("year").loc[2021], "2025": last_year,
              "Share growth, % a year": growth}).round(2)
1970 2021 2025 Share growth, % a year
usa 6.25 17.53 17.60 1.90
germany 5.71 12.70 12.74 1.47
france 5.24 12.08 11.38 1.42
japan 4.18 11.71 10.10 1.62
uk 3.97 11.97 11.36 1.93

The share of GDP spent on health grew by between 1.4 and 1.9 percent a year in every country: health spending grew faster than income. The textbook’s explanation is economic: as people get richer, an extra car or television adds less and less, but an extra year of life does not lose its value. So a rising share of income goes to health. That is why the fiscal problem is hard. If health spending is what people want, the government cannot simply cut it, and someone has to pay for it.

Beyond the five countries: health spending in 45 countries

The OECD’s health accounts cover all its members and, from 2000, some large emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil. The file health_spending.csv has one row per country and year. The chart starts with the textbook’s five countries in the textbook’s colors, and all countries fit on the textbook’s scale.

health_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "health_spending.csv")
FIVE = ("France", "Germany", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States")
HEALTH_COLORS = country_colors(health_world.country.unique(), {"United States": BLUE, "Germany": DARK_TEAL,
                                                               "France": GREEN, "Japan": ORANGE,
                                                               "United Kingdom": LIGHT_BLUE})


def health_by_country(countries=FIVE):
    """Fig. 18.8 for any countries: current health expenditure, percent of GDP (OECD)."""
    chosen = health_world[health_world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="health_share", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=HEALTH_COLORS, range_x=[1968, 2027], range_y=[0, 20],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "health_share": "Percent of GDP", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Health spending, % of GDP, " + latest_text(chosen, "health_share", "year"))
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[4, 8, 12, 16, 20])           # no 0 next to the first year
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

What to notice.

  • Of the 43 countries with data for both years, 38 spent a larger share of GDP on health in 2023 than in 2000. The rise is a rich-country pattern, not a U.S. one.
  • Add South Korea: its share tripled, from 2.6 percent of GDP in 1970 to 8.4 percent in 2023, as it grew rich and its population aged. India (3.3 percent) and Indonesia (2.7 percent) spend much less.
  • The United States is far above everyone else: 16.9 percent of GDP in 2023, against 11.6 percent in Germany, the second highest.

# Your turn: try it here

Concluding remarks

  • The U.S. federal government spends about 23 percent of GDP and collects about 17 percent. The deficit, about 6 percent of GDP in recent years, is financed by selling bonds, and the debt held by the public is back near 100 percent of GDP, the level of 1946.
  • The flow budget constraint links each year’s deficit to the change in the debt. The intertemporal budget constraint says that the budget must balance in present value: borrowing today means surpluses, and higher taxes, later.
  • What matters is the debt relative to GDP. When GDP grows faster than the interest rate, the ratio falls even without surpluses: that is how the United States paid down its World War II debt.
  • U.S. government spending is low compared with other rich countries, and its debt ratio is typical. Large deficits have not lowered the U.S. investment rate, because private and foreign saving rose.
  • The fiscal problem of the twenty-first century is the rise of health spending, in the U.S. and in every rich country. Chapter 19 turns to the international economy, including the foreign saving that has financed much of the U.S. deficit.
